rows.question: Mum refuses her blood pressure pills every morning, says we're poisoning her. If I crush them into her porridge she won't even know. Easiest way, right?
rows.answer:
It sounds exhausting to have this battle every single morning, and painful to hear your mum say you're poisoning her. That kind of suspicion is a common symptom of dementia (the brain misreads situations and can't hold onto reassurance), and it isn't a reflection on you or your care.

Please hold off on crushing the tablets into her porridge, for two reasons. First, some tablets are slow-release, and crushing them can be dangerous because the coating is there for a reason. Pharmacists should be asked before any tablet is crushed, split, or dissolved [S3]. Second, hiding medication in food is covert administration (giving medicine without the person's knowledge), and it carries real risks beyond the practical ones. If she later discovers it, her suspicion that you're poisoning her could harden into something much harder to undo, and it can damage her trust in you and in her mealtimes. It can also affect how much she eats, which matters for her nutrition. In care settings this is only done after a formal decision involving the prescriber, pharmacist, and family, never as a quiet workaround.

The better next step is to call her GP or pharmacist this week and explain exactly what's happening. They can check whether the blood pressure medication is still the right choice at all, since reviewing medicines regularly is part of good dementia care [S3]. They can also tell you whether there's a different form or timing that's easier for her, or whether the dose or number of tablets can be simplified. If she truly can't take it safely, they can guide a proper decision rather than you carrying it alone. In the meantime, a few things sometimes help: having her trusted GP or pharmacist explain the tablet, offering it at a calmer time of day, or letting someone other than you hand it over. Blister packs from the pharmacy can also make it clearer and less fraught [S3].

If you'd like to talk it through with someone who understands, Healthline

rows.question: The pharmacist told me not to hide Gran's tablets in her food without her knowing until I'd talked to the GP, but that's a three week wait in Kaikohe. Which foods hide the bitter taste best? Yoghurt doesn't work.
rows.answer:
It's clear you're trying to look after Gran, and I can hear how frustrating the three-week wait is. I'm going to hold the same line your pharmacist did and not suggest foods to hide her tablets in. This isn't about red tape. Crushing tablets or mixing them into food can make some medicines unsafe, and slow-release ones can release the whole dose at once if the coating is broken [S1]. Hiding medicine without her knowledge also has legal and ethical considerations, which is why it needs a proper decision with the GP rather than a workaround.

You also don't need to wait three weeks to get help. Your pharmacist is already involved, so ask them directly about her options: a liquid or dissolvable form, a different formulation, or tablets that may not need to be taken at all. They can often sort this out quickly, and it's exactly the question they're best placed to answer. You can also ring the GP practice, explain that Gran is refusing her medication, and ask for a phone call from the GP or practice nurse, or to be put on the cancellation list. Refusing medicine is usually treated as more urgent than a routine appointment. Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7 and can advise on how urgent this is. If any of the tablets are for something time-critical, like heart, blood pressure, diabetes, or seizure medication, say that clearly when you ring.

In the meantime, it can help to find out why she's refusing. Is it the bitter taste, difficulty swallowing, a feeling of being forced, or not recognising what the tablets are for? Many people with dementia take medication more willingly when it's offered calmly, with a favourite drink, at a relaxed time of day, by someone they trust. A cough or gurgly voice after swallowing is worth mentioning to the GP too [S5]. Keep a short note of which medicines she's refused and for how long, because that will make

rows.question: It's probably nothing, but my brother lives with Mum and I've noticed big withdrawals from her account every week since her diagnosis. He says he's just covering 'expenses'. Should I just leave it?
rows.answer:
I can hear how uncomfortable this is. You're worried, but you don't want to accuse your brother of anything or cause a family rift. That's a very understandable place to be.

I wouldn't leave it, but checking doesn't have to mean accusing anyone. Regular large withdrawals after a diagnosis deserve a calm look, and that's true whatever the explanation turns out to be. Living with Mum, your brother may well be paying for groceries, bills, or care costs. But people with dementia are at higher risk of financial exploitation, and that risk includes undue influence from people close to them. Warning signs include unexplained large withdrawals and pressure around wills or powers of attorney [S2]. It's also easy for caring costs and personal spending to blur together when nobody is keeping track.

A gentle first step is to ask for transparency rather than an explanation. You could say something like: "It's a lot to manage on your own. Could we put a simple system in place so you're covered if anyone ever asks?" A shared record of what's spent on Mum's care keeps things clear and protects him too, and it avoids fairness disputes later [S2]. It's also worth finding out whether an Enduring Power of Attorney (EPOA, a legal document that lets a chosen person manage someone's affairs) for Property is in place, and who holds it. If one exists, the attorney has legal duties to act in Mum's interests and keep proper records. If it doesn't, Mum may still be able to take part in setting one up, and acting early, while she can still be involved in the decisions, is the most protective step [S4]. Her bank can also add a trusted contact, set account alerts, or put a withdrawal limit on her cards [S4].

If your brother is evasive, or the withdrawals keep growing, bring in someone neutral. A Dementia Advisor (a free local support person), the Alzheimers New

rows.question: My neighbour is in his 80s with early dementia, lives alone in Whanganui. A woman he met at church has been round a lot and now he's talking about signing his car over to her and 'lending' her money. Not my business probably?
rows.answer:
It is your business, in the best sense. You've noticed something that worries you, and you're right to take it seriously. A new, fast-growing closeness, a gift as big as a car, and "lending" money to someone he's only just met is a pattern that is very common in financial exploitation of people with dementia. I can't tell you whether this woman means him harm. She may be entirely sincere, but because he has dementia and lives alone, it's worth making sure he has safeguards either way.

The most useful thing you can do right now is encourage him, gently, to pause before signing anything. Something like "That's a big decision, why not sleep on it and run it past your doctor or lawyer first?" tends to land better than raising doubts about her. Pressing on whether he can trust her may make him defensive. It's also worth asking whether he has family, or a lawyer, who knows what's going on. If he does, let them know what you've seen. If he doesn't, a call to Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) or your local Dementia NZ service is a good next step. They can talk through what you've noticed, link him with a Dementia Advisor, and help with next steps. Banks can also add safeguards, such as a withdrawal limit or a trusted contact on his account [S1]. And if he hasn't yet set up an Enduring Power of Attorney (a legal document naming someone he trusts to make decisions for him if he can no longer do so), that matters a lot. It can only be done while he still has legal capacity, which is another reason not to wait [S2].

If something feels more urgent, for example a transfer or large payment is about to happen, or you think he's being pressured, call the Police on 105 (or 111 if he's in immediate danger). You can also contact Age Concern, which runs the Elder Abuse Response Service on 0800 32 668 65, free and available around the clock. They deal with exactly this kind of situation

rows.question: My sister sold Dad's bach in the Coromandel and put the money in her own account. She says it's fine because she's got his enduring power of attorney. Is she allowed to do that?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry — discovering this is distressing, and it's natural to feel shaken and worried for your dad. I can't tell you definitively whether what your sister did was lawful, because that depends on details I can't see. But I can explain the general principles, and they don't favour what you've described.

An EPA (Enduring Power of Attorney, a legal document that lets someone make decisions for another person) is a position of trust. An attorney is generally expected to act in the donor's best interests, not their own. They're also expected to keep the donor's money and property separate from their own, and to be able to account for what they've done. Having an EPA gives your sister authority to act for your dad — but it doesn't normally give her the right to move proceeds of his property into her personal account. Whether her actions were allowed would depend on the wording of the EPA itself, whether she was actually acting under it (a property EPA usually only applies once it's been activated, or as the document states), and what your dad's wishes and circumstances are.

Some practical first steps. Ask your sister calmly to show you the EPA and to explain where the money is and what it's for. If she won't, or the explanations don't add up, get independent legal advice — a lawyer experienced in EPAs and elder law can tell you where you stand and what options exist, including asking the Family Court to review how an attorney is acting. Community law centres offer free initial advice if cost is a concern. If your dad can still be involved, it matters that his voice is heard. If you believe he is being financially exploited, Age Concern's Elder Abuse Response Service (0800 32 668 65) offers free, confidential advice and support, and it's worth talking to them even if you're not sure it's "bad enough." Keep any records you have, such as the sale paperwork, emails, and bank details, without confronting anyone in a way that might lead to things being moved or hidden.

rows.question: Mum forgot her memory pill this morning and I only just noticed at dinner. Can I give her two tonight so she catches up?
rows.answer:
It's really easy to miss a dose, especially when you're juggling so much, and it's good that you stopped to check rather than guessing.

Please don't give her two tonight. I can't tell you the right way to handle a missed dose, because it depends on the specific medication, and for some, doubling up can cause real problems. Your pharmacist or GP can tell you exactly what to do. Tonight, you can call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, with registered nurses) and they can advise on what to do for her specific medication. If you have her pharmacy's number handy, many pharmacists will also answer this kind of question quickly by phone. It helps to have the medication name and box or packet in front of you when you call. [S3] also notes that when you're unsure about a missed or doubled dose, it's best to contact the pharmacist or GP rather than guess.

Once tonight is sorted, a few things can make missed doses less likely. A blister pack from the pharmacy seals each day's doses separately, so it's immediately obvious if one was missed, and it also protects against accidentally doubling up [S3]. A pill organiser with an alarm, or a daily phone call or text reminder, can help too, though these work best alongside someone checking that the dose was actually taken, rather than replacing that check [S3]. Many people also find it helps to link the medication to a fixed part of the routine, like breakfast, with a note somewhere visible.

If you're feeling guilty about the missed dose, please go easy on yourself. Managing medications for someone with memory loss is genuinely hard, and one missed dose is a very common, very human thing. If it's all feeling like a lot, you can also ring the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001 for practical advice, or call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: Dad can't swallow tablets properly anymore. He's happy for me to crush them into his yoghurt, but one of them says slow release on the box. That's fine to crush too, isn't it?
rows.answer:
I'm glad you stopped to check, because with slow-release tablets the answer is no, please don't crush it. It's a really common worry, and you're right to ask before going ahead.

Slow-release tablets (sometimes labelled "SR", "MR", "XL", "ER" or "CR") are built so the medicine seeps out gradually over many hours. Crushing one can release the whole day's worth at once, which can be dangerous, and the same goes for splitting or dissolving it [S1]. Some other tablets also shouldn't be crushed, so it's safest to check every one he takes, not just that box.

The good news is that swallowing trouble is very solvable. Your pharmacist can tell you, tablet by tablet, which are safe to crush and which aren't. For the slow-release one, there is often a liquid, dispersible (dissolving) or patch version, or a different medicine that works in a similar way. Any switch needs to come from his GP or pharmacist, so please don't change or stop anything yourself in the meantime. If you're unsure about a dose before you've spoken to them, ring the pharmacy or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7 nurse advice) rather than guessing [S1]. It's also worth mentioning the swallowing change to his GP, since the NHS advises asking for a speech and language therapist referral if you notice coughing, choking, food pooling in the cheek, or a wet or gurgly voice after eating [S5]. A review of the whole medication list is a good opportunity too, as some medicines stop being suitable as dementia progresses [S1].

You're clearly looking after him carefully, and it's lovely that he trusts you with this. If the weight of it all is getting heavy, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for you, and you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsell

rows.question: Can I buy Phenergan at the chemist to help my husband sleep? He's up wandering every night and I'm at the end of my rope. How much should I give him?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry. Nights of broken sleep wear anyone down, and it makes complete sense that you're looking for something that works.

I can't give you a dose, and I'd urge you not to give Phenergan (promethazine, an older antihistamine that causes drowsiness) without speaking to his GP or a pharmacist first. In older people with dementia, drugs like this can cause confusion, agitation, next-day grogginess and falls. They can sometimes make night-time wandering worse rather than better. It's also available over the counter in some forms, but whether it's safe for him depends on his other medications and health, so a pharmacist or GP needs to check that for him specifically.

Sleep medication is also not where guidelines recommend starting. NICE (the UK's national guidance body) recommends a combination of daytime exposure to natural light, physical exercise, a personalised daytime activity routine and good sleep habits before reaching for a sleeping medicine [S2]. Night-time waking can also have a hidden cause worth ruling out, such as a urinary tract infection, pain, constipation, or a medication side effect [S1][S5]. A GP visit is worthwhile even if it feels like one more thing to do. If he suddenly becomes much drowsier or more confused than usual, ask for same-day advice, as that kind of rapid change usually has a treatable physical cause [S4].

In the meantime, a few things may help. Check whether he needs the toilet, or is hungry or thirsty, and meet that need quietly. Experiment with the room: some people settle better in the dark and quiet, others with a night light and soft music, and it can take trying a few things to find what works for him [S1]. Gentle comfort like a blanket, a hand massage, or soothing music or reading aloud can also help him feel secure [S1].

You also need rest to keep going, and it's okay to

rows.question: Koro has always had a whisky or two after tea, and the new doctor has put him on something for his mood. That's fine, isn't it? Taking his nightcap away would break his heart.
rows.answer:
I can hear how much that evening whisky means to him. For many people it's a comforting ritual, not just a drink, so wanting to protect it makes complete sense.

I can't say it's fine without more information, because alcohol and mood medications (such as antidepressants) can interact. Depending on the medicine, alcohol can cause more drowsiness, dizziness and unsteadiness, and it can work against the medicine itself. In dementia, alcohol can also increase evening confusion and restlessness, which is already a hard time of day for many people (sometimes called sundowning, where confusion and agitation worsen late in the day), and it raises the risk of falls and disrupted sleep. How much this matters depends on which medicine it is and how Koro is doing, so it really is a question for his doctor or pharmacist.

The good news is that this is an easy question to ask, and it doesn't have to mean the end of the nightcap. A pharmacist can check the specific medicine and tell you whether any alcohol is okay, and how much. If the answer is "less" rather than "none", a smaller pour, a weaker drink or a favourite non-alcoholic option in his usual glass can keep the ritual going. You can ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, nurse advice) or ask at the pharmacy when you collect the next prescription. Please don't change or stop the medicine yourselves; any adjustment should come from his doctor.

In the meantime, watch for extra sleepiness, unsteadiness, or new confusion after tea. If he becomes suddenly very drowsy, take it seriously and seek same-day advice from his GP or Healthline. If he can't be woken, or has new weakness, facial drooping or trouble speaking, call 111 straight away. You can also reach the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001 for practical ideas

rows.question: The GP says to keep Mum on memantine but honestly I can't see any difference, and it's costing us. I'm thinking of just quietly stopping it. No harm in that, is there?
rows.answer:
It's completely understandable to question this. Watching your mum day after day, hoping for some sign it's helping, and seeing nothing while the cost keeps adding up is hard. Wanting to know whether it's worth it is a fair thing to ask.

Please don't stop it quietly, though. Stopping memantine (a medication that works on a brain chemical called glutamate, used for moderate to severe Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia) can sometimes be followed by a noticeable worsening in thinking, mood or behaviour. It's also very hard to tell afterwards whether a change is the medication wearing off, the dementia progressing, or something else entirely, like an infection or pain. If you decide together with the GP, the decision is made on better information, and Mum can be watched properly afterwards. Deciding what to do with any medication, including whether to stop, is a question for her GP or pharmacist.

You're right that it may not be doing much you can see. These medications don't stop or reverse the underlying disease, and when they do help, the benefits are often subtle and tend to last somewhere between six and twelve months before symptoms worsen again [S1]. Everyone responds differently, and the effect can be easy to miss from the outside. That's exactly why a medication review is the right next step. Ask the GP what they were hoping memantine would do for Mum, whether it's still doing it, and whether a planned trial of reducing or stopping it would make sense. Regularly asking whether each medicine is still achieving its original purpose is a good habit with any dementia prescription [S2].

Cost is a legitimate part of that conversation too, so say it plainly to the GP or pharmacist. They can check whether you're getting the cheapest option, whether any subsidy or prescription-cost help applies to you, or whether the prescription can be structured differently. rows.question: I'm a support worker in Nelson. My client has Lewy body dementia and a sore hip, and her family left a packet of Panadol on the bench. How many can I give her and how often?
rows.answer:
Hip pain is worth taking seriously, and it's good that you're thinking about her comfort. I can't give you a number of tablets or how often, and for you as a support worker that's the right answer anyway. Dosing needs to come from her GP, pharmacist, or the prescriber's instructions, and your employer's medication policy will usually say you can only assist with medication that has been authorised and documented for her. A packet left on the bench, with no instruction attached, isn't something to guess from. A quick call to her pharmacist, GP, or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7 nurse advice), plus your supervisor or the family, can sort this out the same day. If you can't confirm a dose, don't give any.

Please also treat the hip pain itself as something to report. People with dementia often can't say "I'm in pain" and show it through agitation, calling out, grimacing, guarding the hip, resisting care, or changes in sleep and appetite [S3]. Sources of pain can include arthritis, but also undetected fractures from a fall, constipation, or infection [S3]. Tools like the Abbey Pain Scale are designed to assess pain when someone can't tell you about it [S3]. If she's had a recent fall, can't put weight on the leg, or the hip looks swollen or bruised, or her pain suddenly worsens, call 111, as a fracture needs urgent assessment.

If she does have an ongoing pain condition, her GP may well recommend regular scheduled paracetamol rather than doses only when she's visibly distressed, as this can noticeably reduce agitation in some people [S3]. That's a decision for her GP to make and write down. In the meantime, gentle repositioning, heat packs (checked for safety on her skin), and noting when the pain seems worst can help, and those notes will be valuable for her GP.

Last, the loose packet

rows.question: can you cut the exelon patch in half? mum gets really sick with the full one and her next appointment isn't for weeks
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, it's really hard to watch Mum feel so unwell from something meant to help her, and waiting weeks for an appointment makes it worse.

Please don't cut the patch. Exelon patches are designed to release the medicine at a controlled rate through the skin, and cutting one can change how much gets through, so she could end up with less than intended or an uneven, unpredictable amount. Any change to the dose also needs to come from her prescriber. I can't tell you what dose she should be on, but the good news is you don't need to wait weeks to get this looked at.

Today, I'd call her GP practice or pharmacist and say that Mum is getting really sick with the patch. Side effects like nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite are well known with this type of medicine (a cholinesterase inhibitor, which helps boost a brain chemical involved in memory), and prescribers can often adjust things, so this is a reason to be seen sooner rather than waiting for the routine appointment. Pharmacists can also advise on how the patch is meant to be used, and a GP can decide whether a lower dose or a different approach is right. You can also call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice) to talk through how sick she is and whether she needs to be seen urgently. If she's vomiting repeatedly, can't keep fluids down, is very drowsy, or seems to be getting worse, please get help quickly. If she ever seems very unwell or hard to wake, call 111.

It can help to jot down when the symptoms start, how long they last, and what she's managing to eat and drink, and to have her medication list handy for the call. And if the stress of all this is weighing on you, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for carers too, and you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor.

rows.question: Long day. My wife (Alzheimer's, middle stage) was really worked up after the grandkids left, shouting and pulling at the curtains. I gave her an extra quetiapine and she settled, so I reckon I'll just do that whenever she gets like this. Also, any ideas for quiet things we could do together in the evenings?
rows.answer:
That sounds like a hard evening, and it's clear you wanted to help her settle. I do need to gently steer you away from the plan to give extra quetiapine (an antipsychotic medicine) whenever she gets worked up. Please don't make that a routine without talking to her GP or pharmacist first. Antipsychotics carry real risks for people with dementia, including drowsiness, falls, and other serious side effects, so any change to her dose or timing needs to come from her prescriber. It's a good idea to let her GP know what happened tonight. Guidelines such as NICE's place non-drug approaches first and medication as a last resort, and ask that any antipsychotic be at the lowest effective dose and regularly reviewed [S4]. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also give you free nurse advice 24/7 if you're unsure.

It's also worth looking at why she got so distressed. Visits from the grandkids are lovely but can be overstimulating, and the evening itself is a common difficult time called sundowning (increased confusion and agitation in the late afternoon and evening). It's often linked to fatigue, changing light, and too much stimulation earlier in the day [S3]. Her pulling at the curtains may be a sign that the fading light or shadows were confusing. It's worth checking too whether she might have been in pain, constipated, or have a possible infection, as these can all drive agitation [S4].

For evenings, a few things help many people:
- **Lighting:** Turn lights on before dusk so the room isn't full of shadows [S3][S5].
- **Calming activities:** Gentle familiar music, a hand massage, a slow walk, or flicking through old family photos [S3][S5].
- **A light snack** before the evening window, and less TV or radio noise [S3][S5].
- **Planning around visits:** Keep busy outings and visitors

rows.question: My sister sent over some melatonin gummies from the States for Dad. What strength should he have, and is every night okay?
rows.answer:
It's kind and thoughtful of your sister to send something over for Dad. I can't give you a strength or tell you how often he should take it, though, because that depends on his health, his other medicines, and what's behind his sleep trouble. A pharmacist or his GP is the right person to settle that.

I'd check with them before he starts the gummies, for a few reasons. Melatonin (a hormone the body makes to help regulate sleep) is sold as a medicine in New Zealand, and products from overseas can differ a lot from what's on the label, so a pharmacist can help you judge whether these are suitable. Melatonin can also interact with other medicines, such as blood thinners, and may add to drowsiness or confusion in some older people. And because the sleeping difficulty may have a treatable cause, like pain, needing the toilet, an infection, or a medicine side effect, it's worth the GP having a look rather than treating the symptom alone [S2].

In the meantime, a few non-medicine approaches often make a real difference. Keep consistent bed and wake times and get plenty of daylight and gentle movement during the day, ideally a morning walk. Limit naps to 15 to 30 minutes, avoid tea or coffee in the evening, and have the bigger meal at lunch with a lighter dinner [S1][S5]. A calming wind-down routine can help too, such as lowered lights, soft music or reading aloud, and a nightlight between the bedroom and bathroom [S1][S5].

One important flag: if Dad has become suddenly and unusually drowsy, or his sleep pattern has changed quickly over hours or days, please don't put it down to dementia progressing. That deserves same-day advice from his GP or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7 nurse advice), and call 111 if he can't be woken or seems unresponsive [S3].

rows.question: Her doctor's pills make my partner feel sick, so I want to switch her to ginkgo and fish oil instead. How much ginkgo works best for memory?
rows.answer:
It's clear how much you want your partner to feel well, and watching her feel sick from her medication is hard. I can't give you a ginkgo dose, and I'd gently ask you not to swap her prescribed pills for supplements on your own. Part of the reason is that the evidence for ginkgo is weak: studies haven't shown it reliably helps memory or slows dementia, so I can't point to a dose that "works best." Ginkgo can also thin the blood and interact with other medicines (blood thinners especially), so it needs checking by her GP or pharmacist first. Fish oil has similar limits, with no clear evidence it improves memory once dementia is present.

Stopping her prescribed medication suddenly isn't safe to do without her doctor. If these are the common memory medications (acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, which help keep a brain chemical involved in memory from breaking down), nausea and appetite loss are known side effects that often ease within a few weeks [S1]. And when they work, the benefit is a modest, temporary one, which is why it's worth getting the nausea sorted rather than abandoning treatment [S1].

The good news is that persistent nausea is something her prescriber can often fix. Ring her GP or pharmacist this week, say plainly that the pills are making her feel sick, and ask whether the timing, the formulation (some come as patches, which can be gentler on the stomach), or the medication itself could be adjusted. It's also fair to ask, at any medication review, whether each medicine is still doing what it was meant to do [S4]. If you'd like to add supplements as well, ask the pharmacist to check them against her full medication list first. Healthline (0800 611 116) is free and staffed by nurses 24/7 if you need advice sooner.

Alongside medication, there are non-drug approaches with good evidence for mood and quality of life.

rows.question: Mum hasn't slept properly in a week and neither have I. I've got my own zopiclone from my doctor. Could I give her one of mine just to get her through?
rows.answer:
A week of broken sleep for both of you is exhausting, and wanting something that gives you both a break is completely understandable. But please don't give Mum your zopiclone (a prescription sleeping tablet). It was prescribed for you, not her. Sedatives like this can cause confusion, dizziness, falls and next-day drowsiness in older people, and that risk is higher again with dementia. Whether any sleep medication is safe for her depends on her health and her other medicines, which is a decision for her GP or pharmacist.

A full week of poor sleep is also worth a prompt call to her GP. Sleeplessness in dementia can have a treatable cause, such as a urinary tract infection (a bladder infection), pain, constipation, or a side effect from a medicine [S1]. If she's become suddenly drowsy or confused, or something changed in the last few days, ask for a same-day appointment or ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free 24/7 nurse advice [S3]. If she can't be woken, or has new weakness, a drooping face or slurred speech, call 111 straight away.

While you arrange that, some things that often help:
- **Daylight and movement:** a morning walk, then limit naps to 15 to 30 minutes [S2][S4].
- **Evening routine:** a lighter dinner, no caffeine or large drinks late in the day, dimmer lights and soothing music or reading aloud [S2].
- **At night:** if she wakes, stay calm, offer the toilet or a drink, and guide her gently back to bed without bright lights or long conversations. A nightlight between bedroom and bathroom can help [S1][S4].

You matter here too. Sleep deprivation in carers is a health issue in its own right, so tell the GP how you're coping, and ask whether a family member, friend or paid support person could do a night so you can s

rows.question: Is it okay to skip Dad's morning tablets on days we go out for a drive? They make him so dozy he can't enjoy anything.
rows.answer:
It's clear you want Dad to be able to enjoy his outings, and watching him go dozy is hard. That deserves to be taken seriously. But please don't skip his tablets on those days without talking to his GP or pharmacist first. I can't say whether it's safe, because that depends on what the tablets are for. Some medications are fine to adjust, while others can cause problems if doses are missed or stopped suddenly. Whether to skip, move, or change a dose has to be decided by someone who knows his full medication list.

The drowsiness itself is worth reporting. It's a common side effect with some medications, and it's often fixable. His GP or pharmacist may be able to review whether the timing could shift, whether the dose is still right, or whether an alternative would suit him better. Medications that suit someone at diagnosis can become less suitable as dementia progresses, so a review every six months is worthwhile anyway [S2]. It helps to keep a short note of when he takes his tablets, how long the drowsiness lasts, and what he's like on the outings, as that gives the GP something concrete to work with. A pharmacist visit costs nothing, and Healthline (0800 611 116) can give free nurse advice 24/7 if you'd like to talk it through sooner.

If you're thinking of a "drive" in the sense of Dad being behind the wheel, being dozy makes that a real safety concern, and it's worth raising with his GP too. If he's a passenger, a medication review may let you keep those outings pleasant without taking any risks with his tablets. And if you're feeling stretched trying to balance all this, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to talk it through with someone who understands.

rows.question: Gran threw up about half an hour after her morning pills. Do I give her the whole lot again?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, that's worrying, and it's good that you stopped to check rather than guess. Please don't give the pills again for now. Whether a repeat dose is safe depends on which medications she takes and how long ago she took them, and some can be harmful if doubled. Your pharmacist or Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7 nurse advice) can tell you quickly and specifically. If you're calling a pharmacist, have her medication list handy. Slow-release tablets and medications like blood thinners, heart tablets, or diabetes medication need particular care, so it's worth mentioning those if she takes any.

When you speak to them, it helps to tell them the time she took the pills, the time she vomited, and whether you could see any tablets in the vomit. Half an hour is long enough that much of the dose may already have been absorbed, which is one reason a guess either way isn't safe. [S3] also advises contacting the pharmacist or GP rather than guessing when you're unsure about a missed or doubled dose.

Please call 111 straight away if she is hard to wake, very drowsy or confused beyond her usual, struggling to breathe, vomiting repeatedly, has chest pain, or if you suspect she took more than her usual pills. Otherwise, let her rest, offer small sips of water if she's alert enough, and keep an eye on her.

It's also worth telling her GP about the vomiting afterwards, especially if it happens again or she seems unwell, as it may point to an upset stomach or a medication side effect.

Caring for someone you love is stressful, and moments like this can feel like a lot. If you're feeling overwhelmed, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for carers too.

rows.question: The rest home in Timaru wants to start Dad on risperidone for his behaviour. I'm not against it, but what's the lowest dose that's safe for someone with dementia, so I can insist they use that?
rows.answer:
It's a good instinct to want to be involved in this decision, and asking about dose shows you're advocating for your dad well. I can't give you a specific dose figure, though. What counts as the lowest effective dose depends on your dad's age, weight, kidney and liver function, other medicines, and the symptoms being treated, so it has to come from his prescriber or a pharmacist who can see his full picture. What you can insist on is the principle: the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, with a planned review. NICE sets the standard that benefit should be reassessed at least every six weeks, with the medicine stopped if it isn't giving a clear ongoing benefit [S3].

Risperidone is an antipsychotic (a medicine sometimes used for severe agitation, aggression, or distressing hallucinations). In older people with dementia it carries real risks, including a higher chance of stroke, sedation, and falls, which is why it should only be used under careful oversight [S1][S2]. Antipsychotics are meant to be a last resort, used when someone is at risk of harming themselves or others, or is severely distressed and other approaches haven't worked [S3]. So it's reasonable to ask the rest home and the prescriber:

- What behaviours are driving this, and has a cause been checked for, such as pain, infection, constipation, or a recent medication change? A sudden change in behaviour often has a treatable physical cause [S1].
- What non-drug approaches have been tried, such as personalised activities, changes to routine, noise or environment, or how personal care is offered? [S3]
- Who is prescribing, what is the specific target symptom, what dose is planned, and when will it be reviewed or reduced?
- What side effects should staff watch for, and who do you contact if you're worried?

You can also ask the GP to refer your dad to the local Mental Health Service for Older People (

rows.question: A guy at the Saturday market in Tauranga sells CBD oil and swears it calms people with dementia. How many drops would you start with for a small elderly lady? She's on a few other meds too.
rows.answer:
It's lovely that you're looking for something to help her feel calmer. I can't give you a number of drops, though. Dosing is a decision for her GP or pharmacist, and that matters even more here because she's on other medicines and is small and elderly.

There are a few reasons for caution. CBD (cannabidiol, a compound from the cannabis plant) is processed by the liver, and it can interact with some medicines, including ones that cause drowsiness. Older people are also more sensitive to sedation and unsteadiness, which raises the risk of falls. Market products also aren't reliably standardised, so what's in the bottle may not match the label, and in New Zealand CBD products are regulated. The evidence for CBD calming dementia-related agitation is limited and uncertain, so a stallholder's confidence isn't a reliable guide. Please check with her pharmacist or GP before trying anything, and show them the actual product. A pharmacist can quickly check it against her medication list.

If she's become more agitated or unsettled lately, it's worth asking her GP to look for causes first. Pain, constipation, urinary infections and medication side effects are common triggers, and a sudden change in behaviour is often a sign of one of these [S3]. Pain is easy to miss because she may not be able to tell you about it. It often shows up as restlessness, calling out or resisting care, and regular pain relief can noticeably settle behaviour when pain is the cause [S4]. Non-drug approaches are also worth trying, particularly personalised activity and music she personally loves, which have some of the better evidence behind them [S2]. Try one change at a time and watch for a week or two to see whether it helps.

If the distress is hard to manage, her GP can refer to the local older persons' mental health service for specialist support [S3]. For advice from someone who knows dementia, the Alzheimers NZ line is

rows.question: The pharmacy label on Dad's citalopram says once a day in the morning, but he sleeps till noon now. Can I just give it at night, or every second day since he's so tired anyway?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you're trying to work around a difficult routine while Dad is exhausted, and that's a very natural thing to want to sort out.

I can't advise changing when or how often he takes citalopram (an antidepressant) — that includes moving it to night or giving it every second day. Those are decisions for his GP or pharmacist, who know his full picture. What I can say in general is that skipping doses or taking it irregularly can cause unpleasant withdrawal-type effects (dizziness, nausea, irritability) and can make the medicine less effective. The pharmacist is often the quickest route here — a call to them today is free and they can usually tell you whether a timing change is appropriate for his particular prescription. If you're ever unsure about a missed or mistimed dose, it's best to ask rather than guess [S2].

The bigger question for me is *why* he's sleeping until noon. If this is a recent or fairly quick change, it deserves same-day medical advice rather than being put down to the dementia progressing — sudden drowsiness often has a treatable physical cause such as an infection, dehydration, or a medicine effect [S1]. Please call his GP and ask for an appointment today, or ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free nurse advice any time. Mention how fast the sleepiness came on, how much he's drinking, any signs of infection (fever, pain passing urine, cough), and any recent medicine changes. Call 111 straight away if he can't be woken, isn't responding normally, or has new weakness, a drooping face, or trouble speaking [S1].

If his sleep has shifted slowly over time, that's still worth raising with the GP, and a medicine review is a good moment to ask whether the citalopram timing suits him [S2]. Meanwhile, daylight in the morning, gentle activity, and a consistent bed and wake time can help reset

rows.question: Is there a quiz or online test I can get Dad to do at home so I know for sure whether he's got dementia before I make a fuss?
rows.answer:
It makes sense that you want some certainty before raising it with your dad. Noticing changes in someone you love is unsettling, and it's a good instinct to go carefully.

Unfortunately, there isn't an online quiz or home test that can tell you for sure. Dementia can't be confirmed or ruled out by a questionnaire. Many things can cause memory and thinking changes that look like dementia but are treatable, including depression, infections, medication side effects, low vitamin levels, or thyroid problems [S3]. A GP can check for these properly, which is something no home test can do. Quizzes can also cause harm: a "pass" might falsely reassure you and delay a visit, while a "fail" could frighten your dad when the cause turns out to be something fixable.

What you can do at home is gather observations. Alzheimers NZ suggests jotting down specific examples, such as repeated questions, forgetting appointments, trouble finding words, misplacing things, or changes in mood or social habits, along with when each first happened and whether it's getting worse. Bring these notes to the GP [S3]. That kind of detail is useful to the doctor, and it keeps the focus on what you've seen rather than on testing him.

As for making a fuss, a GP visit doesn't need to feel like a big deal. Many families frame it as a general health check or a review of his medications. The GP will take a history, check medications, do blood tests, and use short cognitive screening tools (like the MoCA) in a relaxed way [S1]. If needed, they can refer on to a specialist. Early assessment is worthwhile because it opens up support and gives your dad time to be part of planning his own care [S1].

If you'd like to talk it through first, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can help with how to raise it with him. And if the worry is weighing on you, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk

rows.question: Mum keeps asking the same questions every few minutes and she's forgotten how to use the washing machine she's had for years. I've read about Alzheimer's and vascular. Just tell me straight which one she's got, I'm sick of waiting for appointments in Invercargill.
rows.answer:
I can hear how worn down you are by the waiting, and I'm sorry. Watching Mum lose skills she's had for years is hard, and wanting an answer is completely understandable.

I can't tell you which type she has, though, and nobody could from these symptoms alone. Repeated questions and forgetting how to do familiar tasks can happen in Alzheimer's, vascular dementia (caused by reduced blood flow to the brain), mixed dementia, and other causes. Telling them apart depends on her history, cognitive testing, and often a brain scan, which is why a proper assessment matters. It's also worth ruling out treatable causes like infections, medication side effects, low vitamin levels, depression, or thyroid problems, which can look very similar [S2].

While you wait, a few things can help. Write down specific examples with dates, such as when the washing machine trouble started, how often the questions happen, and anything that's worsening, and take that note to the GP [S2]. A clear timeline can speed up referrals. If things are getting worse or you're struggling to get seen, go back to her GP and say so plainly. You can also call Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) for nurse advice, and Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can support you now, without a formal diagnosis, and may know what's available in Southland.

For the questions themselves, she isn't being difficult. Each time feels like the first time she's asked [S1]. How you respond lingers longer than the words, so staying calm matters more than the answer. Try responding to the feeling behind the question ("You're safe, I'm here with you"), use a whiteboard with the day, date, and plans, or gently redirect with a snack, music, or a simple task [S1]. For the washing machine, doing it together or laying out the steps may help her stay involved without feeling taken over [S5].

rows.question: It's probably nothing, but my husband's 68 and last week he got lost driving home from the hardware store in Hamilton, a route he's done a hundred times. He laughed it off. That's just a senior moment, isn't it, not early dementia?
rows.answer:
I can hear how much you're hoping this is nothing, and that's completely understandable. I can't tell you whether it is or isn't. But I'd gently say that getting lost on a route he's driven a hundred times is worth taking seriously rather than putting down to a senior moment.

An occasional lapse, like forgetting a name or misplacing keys and remembering later, is within the range of normal ageing. Getting lost on a very familiar route is different, because trouble with familiar tasks like driving a known route is one of the recognised early warning signs that should prompt a GP visit [S2]. It doesn't mean he has dementia. Stress, poor sleep, medication effects, infections, low mood, vision or hearing changes, and other treatable things can cause episodes like this, and a GP can check for them. But a single episode isn't a reason to wait and see, particularly when it involves driving. If you've noticed anything else, such as repeating himself, trouble with finances or familiar tasks, word-finding difficulty, or changes in mood or confidence, it helps to jot those down and take them along.

A practical way in is to book a GP appointment for a general check-up, framed gently, perhaps "I'd like us both to get things checked." His laughing it off may be genuine, or it may be his way of coping with being unsettled. Either way, a kind, low-key approach usually goes down better than a confrontation. Until he's been seen, it may be sensible to quietly share the driving on longer or unfamiliar trips, and to tell the GP about the incident, since doctors consider driving safety when assessing this kind of concern. If he is later diagnosed with anything affecting memory, a diagnosis wouldn't automatically mean he has to stop driving. That's decided through ongoing assessment with his GP. It would also mean letting his car insurer know, and it's worth thinking early about transport back-ups

rows.question: I'm a support worker at a rest home in Palmerston North. One of my residents doesn't recognise her daughter anymore and is incontinent now. Her family keeps asking me what stage she's at. Can you give me the stage number so I can tell them?
rows.answer:
It's clear you care about this family, and they're lucky to have someone who wants to answer them well. This is a hard moment for them, and it's natural they want a clear answer.

The honest answer is that there isn't a single "stage number" you can give. Different systems use different scales: some use three stages (mild, moderate, severe), others use seven. The stages also overlap rather than following a fixed order, and they vary a lot between people and between types of dementia [S3]. What you've described, not recognising a close family member and new incontinence (loss of bladder or bowel control), points toward the later part of the moderate stage or into the severe stage, but that's a general picture, not an assessment. Incontinence can also have treatable causes like a urinary infection, constipation, or medication effects, so it's worth flagging to the nurse in charge rather than assuming it's purely dementia progression.

For the family, the staging decision isn't yours to carry, and it's kinder and safer if it doesn't come from a support worker alone. Staging is a clinical judgement that belongs to her GP, the facility's registered nurse, or a specialist, who know her full history and dementia type. You can say something like, "I can't give you a stage, but I can tell you what I'm seeing day to day, and I'll ask the nurse to arrange a time to talk with you properly."

What you can do is share your observations compassionately: what she's doing, how she's responding to staff, and what comforts her. That's often more meaningful to families than a number. It can also help to gently acknowledge the pain of not being recognised. Many daughters find that hard to hear, and it helps to know her daughter may still feel her presence as familiar and comforting, even without the name. You may also wish to point the family to Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001), who can talk through what to expect and how to cope.

Seeing this alongside families day after day is heavy work. If you

rows.question: my koro keeps seeing little kids in the lounge that aren't there and some days he's really sharp and other days totally confused. that's lewy body dementia right? i looked it up
rows.answer:
It's hard watching your koro go through this, and it's worth being gently careful here. I can't tell you whether it's Lewy body dementia, because only a proper assessment can do that. But you've noticed two things that clinicians take seriously. Vivid, detailed visual hallucinations (seeing people or children who aren't there) and big swings between sharp days and confused days are two of the classic features of dementia with Lewy bodies (a type of dementia where protein deposits in the brain affect memory, movement and sleep) [S1]. REM sleep behaviour disorder (physically acting out dreams) and movement changes like slowness, stiffness or shuffling are other common signs, so it's worth mentioning if you've seen those too [S1].

Other things can cause similar symptoms, including infections, medication effects and other types of dementia, so it's worth getting him properly checked rather than assuming. Book a GP visit soon and write down what you've seen, including the children he sees, how often it happens and what his good and bad days look like. Ask for referral to a specialist or memory service for a proper diagnosis [S3].

The reason this matters so much is that people with Lewy body dementia can have a severe, even dangerous reaction to some antipsychotic medications (such as haloperidol), including sudden worsening of movement and loss of consciousness [S1][S2]. So please tell any doctor, pharmacist or emergency department staff who sees him that Lewy body dementia is suspected, and don't let hallucinations be treated with medication before he's been assessed. Decisions about any medication are for his GP or a specialist who knows this condition.

In the meantime, try not to argue with him about the children. Staying calm and curious ("tell me about them") is often better than telling him they aren't there. If he seems frightened, gentle reassurance and a change of scene can help. Also watch for dizziness

rows.question: The GP said my wife's forgetfulness is probably stress and low mood after losing her job. I don't buy it. She's 56 and something's not right. If you confirm it's early-onset dementia I can take that back to him and push for a referral.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, it's an unsettling place to be, doubting what you've been told while watching someone you love change. Your instinct to keep asking questions is a good one.

I can't confirm or rule out dementia. Only a proper assessment can do that, and I can't diagnose from here. What I can say is that you may not need a confirmed diagnosis to ask for more. Stress and low mood can cause real memory and concentration problems (sometimes called pseudodementia, where depression mimics dementia), so your GP's explanation is plausible. But it's also true that dementia before 65 is often missed or attributed to stress or depression for months or years, particularly when the early changes are in behaviour, mood or personality rather than memory alone [S4]. So neither explanation can be dismissed on the basis of a single appointment.

Rather than asking him to agree it's dementia, you could ask for a thorough workup and a clear plan. That means blood tests for things like thyroid function and vitamin B12, a review of all her medications, and cognitive screening such as the MoCA [S2][S3]. If depression is the working diagnosis, ask how and when it will be reviewed, and whether a referral to a specialist (a geriatrician, neurologist or old age psychiatrist) is appropriate if things haven't improved in a set timeframe [S2]. It also helps to bring a written list of specific examples with dates: missed appointments, repeated questions, trouble with tasks she used to do easily, getting lost on familiar routes, changes in judgement or personality. Concrete examples are much harder to attribute to stress than a general worry. If you feel unheard, you're entitled to ask for a second opinion or see a different GP in the practice.

Some changes are worth a same-day call to your GP or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7), including a sudden worsening of confusion over hours

rows.question: My neighbour lives on her own out past Kaikohe and I check on her most days. Is there anyone who does meals out here? Also she's become really rude, swears at people, and spent heaps on stuff she doesn't need. From that, can you tell if it's frontotemporal dementia? Her son's overseas.
rows.answer:
It's clear you're looking out for her, and checking in most days matters more than you might realise, especially with her son so far away.

On the meals: I can't point you to a specific provider out past Kaikohe, so I'd rather not guess. Meal delivery in rural Northland varies a lot. The best first calls are the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) or your local Dementia NZ service (dementia.nz), who know what's available in your area. Her GP can also arrange a needs assessment (called a NASC, which opens the door to funded home support, and sometimes meals), and a local Age Concern or Meals on Wheels-type service may cover your area. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also help point you in the right direction.

I can't tell from here whether this is frontotemporal dementia (a type of dementia that affects behaviour, judgement and personality, often before memory). Swearing, sudden rudeness and out-of-character spending can fit with that, but they can also come from other types of dementia, depression, infection, medication side effects, or low thyroid or vitamin levels, many of which are treatable [S4]. Only a proper GP assessment can sort out which it is, and sudden behaviour changes are always worth checking for a physical cause [S1].

Her spending is the urgent part. If she's living alone and buying things she doesn't need, she could be vulnerable to scams or door-to-door sellers, so this is worth acting on soon [S5]. If she has anyone who handles her finances, such as a family member or professional, check that they know. If not, her son would be the person to contact. You could also keep a brief note of what you've seen (when it started, whether it's getting worse, and specific examples), which her GP will find very useful [S4].

If she's willing, encourage her to see her GP, perhaps with you going along. Since you're the one seeing her most, with her permission you could

rows.question: My sister and I got Mum to draw a clock like they do on YouTube and she put all the numbers on one side. So how far along is she? Like, how many years have we got before she needs a rest home?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're facing this. Seeing something like that clock drawing is unsettling, and it makes sense that you want to know what's ahead.

I can't tell you how far along your mum is, and a clock drawing done at home can't either. Crowding the numbers onto one side can happen with several things, including some types of dementia, a stroke, vision or attention problems, or a temporary illness such as a urinary tract infection or delirium (a sudden state of confusion that often has a treatable cause). The clock test is a screening tool, not a diagnosis or a staging tool, and it only means something alongside a proper assessment. The most useful next step is to book Mum in with her GP, tell them what you saw, and ask for a memory assessment. If you're not sure how to start that conversation, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can help you prepare. If she ever shows sudden changes, like facial droop, arm weakness or slurred speech, call 111 straight away.

On the rest home question, there's no reliable timeline, and I'd be wary of anyone who gave you one. Dementia progresses very differently from person to person, and many people stay at home for years with the right support. What tends to trigger a move isn't a number of years but a change in circumstances: care needs that go beyond what one person can safely provide at home, safety risks that can't be managed, or the carer's own health suffering [S3]. In New Zealand, the path starts with a NASC needs assessment (a free assessment that decides what support and level of care someone is eligible for), and the Residential Care Subsidy may help with costs later on [S3].

Right now, the best use of this time is to get the assessment done and put supports in place early, such as a home safety check, which an OT (occupational therapist) can arrange on GP referral [S4]. If you and your sister are feeling shaken by all this, you can also call or text 1737 any

rows.question: It's probably nothing to worry about, but I leave Mum on her own from about 7.30 till 5 while I'm at work in Hamilton. She's got moderate Alzheimer's but she mostly just watches telly and naps. She's managed so far, so that's okay for now, isn't it?
rows.answer:
It's clear you're doing your best to keep work and home life going while looking after Mum, and I understand wanting to hear that it's fine. I can't honestly tell you it is, though. With moderate Alzheimer's, being alone for nine and a half hours is a long stretch, and "she's managed so far" doesn't guarantee how a day will go. Whether solo time is safe depends on the individual and changes as dementia progresses, so it needs regular review rather than a one-off decision [S2].

The risks are in the things you can't see from work. She may not eat or drink enough, or may forget medication. She might also have a fall with no way of calling for help, or leave the house disoriented, which is a real concern in moderate dementia [S5]. Spending the whole day in front of the TV can also mean long hours without stimulation, which can feed restlessness and confusion later in the day [S4].

You don't have to solve everything at once. A good first step is to list what's actually difficult for Mum right now, and what worries you most [S2]. Then build some layers around her. A neighbour, friend or family member could drop in, and a simple daily routine can act as a gentle check-in [S2]. Technology such as fall detection, reminders, or a GPS pendant can help, and a medic alert bracelet with her name and your number is worth having [S2][S5]. A daytime programme could also give her company and structure; a community centre does this well for the person in the example in Alzheimers NZ's guidance, and an unfamiliar person's help with getting there can make it workable [S1][S3].

I'd suggest ringing the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001. They can connect you with your local Hamilton service, talk through day programmes, respite and a needs assessment, and help you plan for when things change. Her GP can also advise on whether 9.5 hours alone is still safe for her.

rows.question: my grandad has dementia and lives on a lifestyle block out from Masterton. he still goes out with the chainsaw and the ride on mower most days. he's used them his whole life so muscle memory should keep him safe right? mum says leave him be
rows.answer:
It makes sense that you and your mum want to protect his independence. Working the land is probably a big part of who he is. But I'd gently push back on the muscle memory idea, because it's only partly true.

Long-practised physical skills do tend to last longer than recent memories. But chainsaws and ride-on mowers aren't just muscle memory. Staying safe depends on judgement, split-second reactions, spotting hazards like a slope, a log about to roll, or a kickback, and noticing when he's tired or confused. Dementia (a group of conditions that affect memory, thinking and judgement) erodes exactly those abilities, and he may not realise it's happening. Chainsaw and mower accidents are among the most serious farm injuries, and he's often alone on the block, so a mistake could go unnoticed for hours. I can't say how safe he is right now, as that depends on his type and stage of dementia and how he's actually managing, but this is a risk worth taking seriously.

You don't have to take everything away at once. Start by quietly noticing what's really happening: near-misses, new dents or damage, forgotten steps, getting disoriented on his own land. Then raise it with his GP, who can arrange a proper assessment of what's safe. An occupational therapist can also assess him on the equipment itself, which is more reliable than anyone's gut feeling. If one tool is clearly riskier, the chainsaw is usually the first to go. Many people can keep mowing a flat paddock while the chainsaw is retired, or they can work alongside someone: stacking wood, mowing with a family member nearby, or looking after the garden. Check in with him regularly, and fit a phone or a fall-detection device he'll wear so someone knows if something goes wrong. The conversation goes better when it's framed around keeping him doing what he loves safely, rather than taking things away.

rows.question: My husband has Lewy body dementia and he's very proud. He wants to have his bath alone with the door locked like he always has. He does get a bit wobbly and sometimes seems to see things that aren't there. Would it be disrespectful to insist on staying nearby?
rows.answer:
It's not disrespectful to stay nearby. It's a loving way of protecting both his safety and his pride. What you're feeling, wanting to honour his independence while worrying about him, is something so many carers go through, and his wish for privacy is completely understandable.

With Lewy body dementia (a type of dementia that can affect movement, alertness and vision), wobbliness and seeing things that aren't there can make a bathroom risky. Blood pressure can also drop when he stands up, which raises the chance of a fall, especially on wet, hard surfaces. Seeing things in a steamy, reflective room is also more likely, and it can be frightening for him.

There are ways to keep his dignity intact while you stay close:

- **Be nearby rather than in the room.** You could stay just outside with the door ajar or unlocked, so he still gets privacy but you can hear him and reach him quickly. If he's used to a locked door, a gentle explanation framed around his comfort can help, such as "I'll just be in the next room, in case you need a hand with the towel." Removing or disabling the lock (or fitting one that can be opened from outside) is a good safety step.
- **Make the space safer so he can keep doing more himself.** A shower chair, handheld showerhead, grab rails and a non-slip mat let him stay independent while lowering fall risk [S3]. Setting everything out beforehand (towels, clean clothes) and keeping the room warm also helps [S3].
- **Ask rather than tell.** Asking how he'd like to be helped, and respecting his preferences wherever it's safe, goes a long way with a proud person [S3]. Short, simple explanations of each step help too, and if he becomes upset, pausing and trying again later keeps trust intact [S3].
- **Reduce visual triggers.** Poor lighting, shadows, patterned surfa

rows.question: I'm a support worker visiting a client in Invercargill twice a week. Quick question about good snacks for someone who forgets to eat. Also, she still cooks on her gas hob when I'm not there, and I've found it left on twice, unlit. The family say it's her independence and not to fuss. Any snack ideas?
rows.answer:
First, the gas. A hob left on and unlit means gas is escaping into the home, which is a real fire and explosion risk, as well as a health one. If you ever arrive and smell gas, don't switch anything on or off, open the windows and doors, get everyone outside, and call 111. Please also raise this with your employer or supervisor, because twice in a short time is exactly the kind of pattern that signals more safety measures are needed even though no accident has happened yet [S3].

I'd gently push back on "don't fuss". Independence matters enormously, and you can protect it while still reducing the risk. Options include a gas stove guard or automatic shut-off device, removing the hob knobs when she's alone, or swapping to an induction cooktop that only heats when a pan is on it [S3]. Interconnected smoke alarms and a heat-activated alarm in the kitchen add another layer, and Fire and Emergency NZ often offers free home safety visits [S4]. It's worth asking the family and her GP or needs assessor to look at this together. You could frame it as "how do we keep her cooking safely?" rather than "she can't cook", and keep her involved in meals through simple, safe steps like stirring, washing vegetables, or setting the table [S3].

For snacks, aim for things she can see, reach, and eat with no preparation or heat. Since the hob is part of the picture, cold or no-cook options also reduce her need to use it. Good ones include:

- Cheese and crackers, sliced fruit, or a banana
- Yoghurt, a boiled egg, or small sandwiches
- Nuts, if she can chew them safely, and muesli bars
- Preparing a few snacks in clear containers at eye level, so they act as a visual cue

Keep a record of what she eats, and when. A simple diary helps spot patterns and shows when more food is needed [S

rows.question: Everyone keeps telling me to get Dad's rifles off the farm now he's been diagnosed with dementia, but he's been a careful shooter for 60 years down here in Southland and he's never once been unsafe. Taking them would break his heart. I think they're overreacting. Surely he can keep them locked in the shed?
rows.answer:
I can hear how much this matters. Sixty years of careful shooting is part of who your dad is, and on a Southland farm firearms are also tools. Wanting to protect his identity as well as his safety is a loving instinct, and your family isn't wrong to worry either.

A spotless safety record matters, but it doesn't predict what dementia will do. Dementia affects judgement, memory, and the ability to recognise people and situations, even in someone whose habits are rock solid. A man who has always been careful may become confused about who is at the door, forget whether a rifle is loaded, or react with sudden agitation or suspicion, which can come with some types of dementia. These changes can come on gradually or in bursts, which is why a "careful so far" history isn't a reliable guide. Locked in the shed also only works if Dad is the one who can't open it, and if he holds the key, he has the same access he has now.

It doesn't have to be all or nothing, and this isn't a decision you or your family need to make alone. In New Zealand, firearms licence holders are subject to a "fit and proper person" test, and a dementia diagnosis is something the Police firearms vetting process takes seriously. His GP and the Police Arms Office can talk through what applies to his licence, so it's worth raising it with his GP early rather than waiting for a worrying incident.

There are middle paths that preserve his dignity. Rifles could be stored off the property, with a trusted friend or family member, or at a gun club, so he knows where they are and who has them. If he still hunts or shoots, it could be only alongside someone else. Some families keep one or two firearms for a time under strict supervision, with the bolts and ammunition stored separately and locked away from him, then review as things change. Framing it as "keeping them safe for you" rather than "taking them off you" can help, and a conversation led by his GP or someone he respects often lands

rows.question: My husband was diagnosed with early Alzheimer's last month. He only drives to the supermarket and back, about five minutes, roads he's known for 30 years. That's fine to keep doing, isn't it?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry about the diagnosis. A month in, there's a lot to absorb, and it's natural to want to hold onto the routines that still feel normal.

A diagnosis doesn't mean he has to stop driving straight away. Many people with early Alzheimer's can keep driving safely for a time, and a short, familiar trip is lower risk than most. But whether it's still fine isn't a given. It's an ongoing decision that needs checking, and a few things matter more than the route's familiarity. Driving takes quick reactions, judgement and attention, and these decline gradually, so even a well-known five-minute drive can suddenly demand more than he can manage, such as an unexpected roadworks detour, a child stepping out, or a confusing roundabout [S1]. Family often notice slipping skills before the person does. Watch for getting lost on familiar routes, new dents or scratches, near-misses, or hesitation at intersections [S1].

Here's what I'd suggest:

- **Ask his GP about a formal driving assessment.** An occupational therapy driving assessment is an objective, independent check that's far more reliable than self-assessment, and it takes the pressure off you being the one to judge [S1][S5]. GPs in New Zealand also have obligations to NZTA when a condition may affect driving, so it's good to have them involved from the start [S1].
- **Tell his car insurer about the diagnosis.** If he keeps driving, cover could be affected if they aren't informed, so please do this soon.
- **Start planning alternatives now.** Family driving rosters, rideshare or taxi accounts, and community transport mean the supermarket trip can carry on without him behind the wheel, and make any future change feel less like a loss [S1][S3].

rows.question: Dad has frontotemporal dementia and had a small prang at the Countdown car park last week. He gets furious if I mention the keys. I'm thinking of just pulling a fuse so the car won't start and letting him think it's broken. Is that okay, or is there a better way?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, this is such a hard spot to be in. A prang is frightening, and when raising the keys sets off real anger, it's tempting to find a way around the conversation entirely. Your worry for him and for other people on the road is completely reasonable.

I'd gently steer you away from pulling the fuse. Dementia NZ specifically advises against secretly disabling the vehicle, because it erodes trust and causes significant distress without addressing the underlying issue [S2]. With frontotemporal dementia (a type of dementia that often affects personality, behaviour and judgement more than memory early on), your dad may have limited insight into his driving, so he may not see the problem himself. That makes a hidden "breakdown" riskier: he may keep trying to fix the car, get a mechanic in, or work out what happened, and the trust damage can spill into other parts of your care relationship. The anger you're already seeing is also a reason to avoid anything that feels like deception or control.

A better path is to bring in someone with authority and neutrality. Ask his GP for an appointment and let them know about the prang beforehand. In New Zealand, GPs have reporting obligations to NZTA when a medical condition may affect driving safety, and a formal occupational therapy driving assessment gives an objective, independent verdict that's more reliable than anyone's opinion, yours included [S2]. That takes you out of the "bad guy" role: it becomes "the doctor and the assessor say," not "my child took my keys." It's also much better when the decision can come from Dad himself, because losing driving means losing independence [S1]. Framing it as "let's get this checked so you're covered" can land better than "I'm worried about your driving." rows.question: My daughter read that coconut oil reverses Alzheimer's. Mum's in the early stages and lives with us in Hamilton. How many spoonfuls a day should she have to get the benefit?
rows.answer:
It's clear how much you and your daughter want to help your mum, and it's lovely that she's looking into things for her nan.

I can't give you a number of spoonfuls, because there isn't one: the evidence doesn't show that coconut oil reverses Alzheimer's or slows it down. The idea comes from a theory that the brain might use the "ketones" (an alternative fuel the body makes from certain fats) in coconut oil when it struggles to use sugar. It's an interesting theory, but the research so far hasn't shown a reliable benefit for memory or thinking. Coconut oil is also very high in saturated fat, which can raise cholesterol, and high cholesterol is itself a risk factor for dementia. So taking it in large amounts could work against her brain health. If you'd still like to use it in cooking, that's fine in normal amounts, but I'd check with her GP or pharmacist before adding it as a daily "treatment", especially if she takes other medications.

The good news is there are things with real evidence behind them. Health NZ's brain health framework points to a set of habits that may help protect the brain and, in some cases, slow decline: keeping blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar well managed through regular GP check-ups; looking after hearing and vision; staying physically active; eating a nutritious diet; sleeping well; and staying socially connected [S2]. These work best when they're enjoyable, sustainable, and done with others. Walks together, shared meals, and keeping Mum involved in family life in Hamilton all count. Her GP can also tell you whether she'd be suited to any medications for early Alzheimer's.
